title: Instinct’s powerful AI assistant is raising privacy and security concerns

reading.body:
Instinct, an AI assistant in private testing that connects to email, messaging, calendars, and device features, was deployed with access to sensitive user data but without adequate safeguards. Users documented that emails were stored in plain text with no deletion option, the service continued operating after being disconnected, and the system could be phished. The failure was one of deploying a system with broad data access before establishing basic security practices.

The system's terms of service granted the company perpetual rights to user data for training and permission to enter binding agreements on users' behalf. This represents a design choice to extract maximum value from user data rather than a technical failure, though it compounds the security lapses. A human review of data handling practices and terms of service before wider testing would have surfaced these issues.

It is not established whether the unauthorized actions users reported reflect a systematic vulnerability or isolated incidents, nor whether the company intentionally designed these data practices or failed to consider them.

reports.title: Instinct’s powerful AI assistant is raising privacy and security concerns

summary:
# Summary

Instinct, an AI personal assistant still in private testing, has generated excitement for its powerful capabilities but is facing significant privacy and security concerns. Created by a team led by former Sierra researcher Noah Shinn, the San Francisco-based tool connects to users' email, messaging apps, calendars, and device features like audio and location to complete tasks such as booking appointments and finding flights. However, users have raised alarms about the company's broad terms of service, which grant Instinct perpetual rights to access, store, and use user data for training purposes, as well as permission to enter into binding agreements on users' behalf.

Multiple testers have documented specific problems, including emails being stored in plain text without deletion options, the service continuing to summarize inboxes after being disconnected, and the tool being easily phishable. Some users reported unauthorized actions, such as Instinct sending emails without permission. After these concerns surfaced, Instinct told the Wall Street Journal it was taking security seriously and announced a $250 million Series B funding round at a $2.5 billion valuation, led by Index Ventures and Benchmark. The company has not yet publicly responded to individual complaints.
